title: How Many Types of Thinking Are There?
author: Terry U
summary: This rigorous survey of the cognitive science of thinking types — from Epstein's anti-computer-brain argument through Kahneman's System 1 and 2, divergent/convergent thinking, and the latest neuroscientific research — offers educators and leaders a practically useful map of the different cognitive operations that 'thinking' encompasses. The article begins with Robert Epstein's influential critique that the computer metaphor for the brain is fundamentally wrong: the brain stores no algorithms, has no software, and does not retrieve static memories but reconstructs experiences dynamically through environmental interaction. From there it surveys the major taxonomies that cognitive science has developed: analytical/logical thinking, creative/divergent thinking, critical thinking, metacognition, and the System 1 (fast, automatic) vs. System 2 (slow, deliberate) framework Kahneman developed in Thinking Fast and Slow. Rather than endorsing any single taxonomy, the article's value is in demonstrating that these different types are genuinely distinct — trainable through different methods, activated by different conditions, and contributing differently to effective reasoning. The practical payoff for educators is a framework for thinking about which cognitive operations a lesson or assignment actually engages, rather than treating 'thinking' as a monolithic outcome that either happens or doesn't.
points: Epstein's anti-computer-brain argument is the article's most important foundational point: if memory doesn't store but reconstructs, if reasoning isn't algorithm retrieval but dynamic assembly, then AI (which does store and retrieve algorithms) is fundamentally different from human cognition — and the implications for how AI and human thinking interact are more complex than most AI-in-education discussions acknowledge.

Kahneman's System 1/System 2 framework is the most practically useful taxonomy for teachers: understanding that most daily cognitive processing is automatic and pattern-matching (System 1) while deliberate analysis is effortful and easily disrupted (System 2) explains why novices need explicit instruction and practice to build automatic competence, not just more time to think.

Divergent and convergent thinking are trainable through different conditions: divergent thinking (generating novel possibilities) is inhibited by evaluation and enhanced by psychological safety and playful contexts; convergent thinking (finding the best single answer) is inhibited by premature closure and enhanced by structured criteria — implications that affect both classroom design and creative professional practice.

Metacognition — thinking about one's own thinking — is the category that most strongly predicts durable learning and transfer: students who can monitor their own comprehension, identify gaps, and regulate their learning strategies outperform those who cannot, regardless of other ability levels, and this skill is explicitly teachable.

The practical reframe for lesson and task design is to ask not 'will students think?' but 'which specific type of thinking does this task engage?' — a question that clarifies whether a lesson is building analytical precision, creative fluency, critical evaluation, or metacognitive monitoring, and whether those are the cognitive operations the learning goal actually requires.
quotes: Robert Epstein’s widely cited argument [ ] has convinced thousands of people that the computer metaphor for the brain is wrong on several fronts. The brain has no software, no algorithms, and no manufactured processors.
Why do we so readily believe that language machines can think? If the brain is not a computer processing a single type of 'data,' then the ways we interact with the world must be equally varied.

No one can experiment on the past, only reconstruct it from what survived, which makes it an exercise in inference under permanent incompleteness. Political and civic reasoning add a constraint neither science nor ethics requires alone: the answer has to be reached with other people who don’t always share premises.

Its first criterion isn’t about the world at all but about the reasoner. Capstone-level “Ethical Self-Awareness” requires a student to discuss in detail both their core beliefs and the origins of those beliefs with depth and clarity.

Scientific thinking is vulnerable to plausibility bias — evaluating evidence by assessing the plausibility of a hypothesized cause, making judgments about the world in ways that are consistent with prior belief — precisely because it’s in constant contact with a messy empirical world that admits of prior expectation. Mathematical thinking has no analogous contamination risk, because it isn’t testing a claim against nature; it’s testing a claim against a closed deductive system.

Creative thinking and magical thinking share surface features. Both traffic in the impossible, the counterfactual, the not-yet-real — and diverge completely on what happens to that material afterward.

Creative thinking asks what else might be possible and then puts the possibility to work; magical thinking picks the possibility up and holds onto it, even when it doesn’t work. None of them are lesser or better versions of “thinking in general.” They are easy to conflate by teaching critical thinking, for example, as if it includes ethical reason, too, or “STEM thinking” as if math and science are one skill.
